arxiv:2611.26444.text: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation. From Yuzhi Huang and colleagues. Robots need to reason from past observations, carry out precise actions, and use the results of those actions to guide what comes next. Mind2Act World tests these abilities separately and together across simulated manipulation tasks, helping identify whether failures come from reasoning, execution, or combining them. The strongest agent succeeded in 52.7 percent of reasoning episodes and 39 percent of execution episodes, but only 12 percent of combined tasks. The results point to linking reasoning and action through environmental feedback as a key challenge.

arxiv:2611.26409.text: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding. From Changli Tang and colleagues. Understanding video alongside its audio remains a major challenge for multimodal systems. WeMM-Video is a family of Chinese-English models that processes text, images, audio, and video, with both quick-response and step-by-step reasoning modes. Across more than one hundred and twenty benchmarks, its largest model sets a new open-source high in combined audio and video understanding, outperforming several proprietary systems and narrowing the gap with Gemini. A nine-billion-parameter model also surpasses a larger open-source competitor.

arxiv:2611.26603.text: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth. From Peiyun Hu and colleagues. Estimating depth from a single camera view often means choosing between sharp edges and consistency across video frames. Depth Pro 2 tackles this by using one scalable network for both images and video, predicting depth at the original image resolution. The approach produces metrically accurate depth maps that are sharp and temporally consistent, outperforming prior methods on all three measures. Its model family also offers different trade-offs among accuracy, sharpness, consistency, and runtime.

arxiv:2611.26595.text: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video. From Yiyan Ji and colleagues. Controlling a video's structure and motion with three-dimensional proxies can improve generation, but the best proxy detail and prompts depend on the task. Coda-DaVinci is an agent-based system that chooses between proxy-guided and direct generation, adjusts proxy detail for each entity, and coordinates simulation with prompts grounded in the proxies. Tests show leading instruction following and scene consistency on two benchmarks, plus better physical plausibility and visual realism than the compared systems. Longer videos gain in event structure and consistency, though transitions and scene-setting adherence remain challenging.

arxiv:2611.26629.text: Posterior Matching Distillation. From Hidir Yesiltepe and colleagues. Diffusion generators can take many iterative steps, and distillation aims to make image and video generation faster without losing the teacher model's range of outputs. Posterior Matching Distillation trains a stochastic student to match teacher estimates of clean images across a range of noise levels, without an extra student scoring network. The method supports different step budgets without retraining and, in experiments on two models, achieves the best Fréchet Inception Distance among four-step methods while remaining competitive on other quality measures.

arxiv:2611.26617.text: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning. From Yuxin Jiang and colleagues. Learning actions from video is difficult because clips show what changes, but not what caused it, so many methods learn the world's dynamics from scratch. O two LaF adapts one pretrained video model for two roles: inferring actions from visual transitions and predicting what happens given an action. It learns both together from unlabeled video through a compact bottleneck. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, it achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and stronger zero-shot transfer across visual contexts and embodiments.

arxiv:2611.26107.text: HiUni: Harmonizing Understanding and Generation in Shared Visual Space. From Jiahao Hu and colleagues. Unified vision models often use separate visual systems for understanding and image creation, limiting how much they share. HiUni extends a pretrained vision-language model by using the same visual encoder and Transformer backbone for both tasks, with task-specific processing only at the output. It adds a pixel-based diffusion head for image creation and a lightweight pathway to restore spatial detail. HiUni matches the pretrained model's average understanding score while performing competitively on image generation and editing.

arxiv:2611.26389.text: ViDecide: Teaching Video Diffusion Models to Reason and Plan Step by Step. From Kaiwen Zhang and colleagues. Video generation models can make realistic clips, yet often break physical or logical rules when planning through several steps. ViDecide treats a video as a sequence of decisions, training models to predict what happens next and when to stop. Its corrective fine-tuning method turns failed decisions toward the model's own successful continuations. Across games and planning tasks, it reached an average strict success rate of eighty-three point eight percent, outperforming prior methods and generalizing to larger puzzles and unseen layouts.

arxiv:2611.26414.text: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain. From Zixuan Huang and colleagues. Vision-language navigation systems often fine-tune their vision-language model on navigation data, which can weaken its general visual abilities. ZeroVLN avoids this by having the model give movement instructions in plain language to a separate action expert. The team first trains the expert to follow those instructions, then improves both parts together through closed-loop reinforcement learning. On standard continuous-environment navigation benchmarks, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms comparable methods while making only minor changes to the model's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities.

arxiv:2611.26516.text: Plan4D: Generative Plannable 4D Worlds. From Hangwei Zhang and colleagues. Predicting future video often produces attractive images but weak physical grounding and inconsistent geometry over time. Plan4D generates future videos from a scene and text-described actions, while also predicting depth, camera views, point clouds, and scene motion. It combines a video generator with a three-dimensional reconstructor and adds a component for predicting scene flow. Tests on synthetic and real-world data show state-of-the-art performance, with improved visual fidelity and geometric accuracy.

arxiv:2611.26380.text: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning. From Yuqi Tang and colleagues. Egocentric video captions can miss brief actions, get their order wrong, or confuse the wearer's movement. EgoCaptioner combines a broad overview with timed descriptions of individual steps, and trains on fifty thousand examples using rewards for accuracy, coverage, timing, and clear narration. Across five benchmarks, it led the evaluated open-source models in caption quality, question answering based on captions, and timing alignment. It also outperformed Gemini three point one Pro on PhysCapBench.

arxiv:2611.25773.text: Duopra: From Full-Duplex Conversation to Full-Duplex Agency. From Chiyu Chen and colleagues. Full-duplex assistants can speak naturally while users talk, but may fail to send tools timely, complete requests, especially after a correction. Duopra trains the assistant to handle task execution as part of the conversation, either by calling tools directly or sending a complete request to a backend. On a benchmark, it raises success with the same backend from four point seven percent to forty-four point seven percent. It also improves tool use and preserves key conversational abilities.

arxiv:2611.25387.text: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs. From Xuwei Ding and colleagues. Spatial reasoning often requires reading a scene, acting on it, then checking what changed, but tests rarely capture that full loop. TuringSpace introduces 125 interactive puzzles that people and multimodal language models solve by clicking and dragging, with new versions generated for training. People solve nearly all the tasks, while the strongest model still fails about one in four. Training a smaller model on the puzzles raises its success rate from 1.6 percent to 33.1 percent and improves results across seven other benchmarks.

arxiv:2611.26510.text: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher. From Guoxin Chen and colleagues. Post-training often relies on successful examples, but those examples can still teach poor habits or miss useful behaviors. AutoMaster uses an artificial intelligence agent to study teacher-model trajectories, write natural-language skill instructions, select data, and improve its interventions using rollout feedback and target-model evaluations. Across terminal, search, and software engineering tasks, it raised mean performance over standard fine-tuning by one point four two to eight point nine nine percentage points. Keeping skill instructions in training also improved mean performance in all six settings.

arxiv:2611.25476.text: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming. From Bo Li and colleagues at National University of Singapore. Adding new skills to a trained neural network usually requires further training, which can be costly and risk disrupting skills it already has. WeightCode uses a frozen language model to write programs that directly change a network's weights, without gradient-based training; the installed skills then run without the language model. The programs enabled new command combinations and pickup actions, and improved ImageNet accuracy by up to seventeen point six two points while preserving existing abilities. They also added robustness across independently trained vision networks, showing that reusable weight programs can build on earlier changes.

arxiv:2611.26590.text: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models. From Jiahao Huang and colleagues. Vision-language models combine images and text, but their answers do not show how concepts are represented inside them. A new method called the Multimodal Concept Lens maps internal states from both modalities into a shared space, making concepts easier to inspect and alter. Experiments show that concepts can be selectively accessed for different tasks and can affect later reasoning. Reliable selective access develops after concept information becomes readable, with similar patterns found across model families and sizes.

arxiv:2611.26286.text: Twice-Told Critiques: Claim-Level Homogenization of Peer Review in the LLM Era. From Ilya Gusev. Peer review works best when readers spot different problems, but critiques are becoming more alike. This study measures overlap in reviews from major conferences and journals, finding year-on-year increases and fewer new problems from a third review at the International Conference on Learning Representations. Reviews flagged as likely written by large language models also overlap more with each other than unflagged reviews. The findings suggest that the range of critiques a paper receives is shrinking.

arxiv:2611.26268.text: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining. From Yingqi Shi and colleagues. Long-context attention can waste computation by giving every query the same number of key-value blocks and by reloading blocks that multiple queries need. LightningMoBA selects blocks with a score threshold, groups work around reused key-value blocks, and overlaps data movement with computation. On Hopper GPUs, it speeds up generation by one point two to one point six times at matched retention. It also raises the mean RULER score from seventy-four point four two to seventy-five point two eight.

arxiv:2611.26248.text: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs. From Yang Wan and colleagues. Testing whether artificial intelligence can design experiments is difficult because the results need to come from real laboratory data. TwinLab-Bench covers fifty-two tasks across physical sciences, life sciences, and engineering, and lets agents design experiments that a laboratory-specific digital twin then carries out using real records. The twin greatly reduces readings that stray from those records and inconsistent answers. Even the strongest model tested scored only forty-five on average, showing that designing reliable experiments remains a challenge.

arxiv:2611.26613.text: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control. From Yiyang Du and colleagues. Robot benchmarks often report only whether a whole task succeeds, leaving unclear how an agent acts and where it goes wrong. AgentRoboCritic analyzes individual actions across twelve manipulation benchmarks, pairing each action with the agent's stated intent and a critic's assessment of the result and failure. The analysis finds strong scene understanding and zero-shot performance, along with some recovery from execution errors, but grasping, alignment, and uneven recovery remain difficult. A fine-tuned critic raises failure-mode accuracy from 32.58 percent to 74.24 percent.

arxiv:2611.26298.text: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions. From Xuankun Rong and colleagues. Everyday tasks can become risky as conversations unfold, especially when important clues appear across earlier messages and images. DailySafe is a benchmark for testing whether multimodal language models can track these changes while still helping with users' legitimate goals. It contains one hundred ninety-five realistic, multi-turn interactions across ten everyday domains, with safety evidence revealed gradually. The benchmark offers a way to evaluate safety in everyday assistance more realistically than tests built around isolated harmful requests.

arxiv:2611.26412.text: How to Effectively Manage the Energy in Residential Systems: Development and Comparison of Methods. From Julian Ruddick. Managing home energy can help cut fossil fuel use, but it requires coordinating electricity use and storage with cleaner power. This work compares simple rules, optimization, and machine learning across three simulations and a real-world test, and introduces TreeC, which learns strategies people can understand. TreeC performed competitively with established methods, but the real-world test showed that unreliable data and unrepresentative training can weaken results. The algorithms cut costs in some homes, though average savings did not cover the cost and effort of putting them in place.

arxiv:2611.25880.text: Evolving Decoding Algorithms for Quantum Error Correction. From Eduardo Dueñez and colleagues. Quantum error correction needs classical decoders that correct noise quickly enough to keep pace with measurements. Researchers describe several belief-propagation decoders in a simple programming language, then use an evolutionary search to find better settings and new decoder designs. Even before the search, damping makes existing decoders seventeen to forty-one times faster at higher error rates. The evolved decoders also improve the balance between speed and errors, and some remain effective across different noise levels, code sizes, and measurement rounds.

arxiv:2611.26546.text: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of H to the 1 elements in a-phi electromagnetic simulation. From Timothy Carlson and colleagues. Time-domain electromagnetic simulations often use smooth finite elements that can give unreliable results, even though edge-based elements better match Maxwell's equations. This work compares the two approaches in an intentionally challenging but physically feasible eddy-current example. The gauge-penalized smooth elements converge to the wrong state, even as the mesh is refined, while a mixed method using smooth and edge-based elements gives reasonable results under general loading conditions.

arxiv:2611.26410.text: Statistical Inference with Ill-Conditioned Random Weight Neural Network Sieves. From Giovanni Ballarin and colleagues. Random weight neural networks fit a regression model using randomly chosen hidden features, but growing the feature set can make the estimation problem badly conditioned. This work develops approximation, estimation, and inference methods that account for this instability, including ridge regularization and a way to assess whether a target direction remains informative. It proves that some approximations can converge faster than Monte Carlo sampling and that valid, studentized inference is possible even as the smallest covariance eigenvalue vanishes.

arxiv:2611.26515.text: Simple Private Noisy SGD is Minimax-Optimal under Population Strong Convexity. From Valentin Roth and colleagues. Private stochastic gradient descent adds noise to protect the data, but it was unclear whether even its simplest form could achieve optimal accuracy on strongly convex problems. This work analyzes a single pass with a fixed step-size schedule and constant batch sizes, under a standard privacy guarantee. For strongly convex generalized linear models, including logistic regression, its error matches the lower bounds for what any private method can achieve. The result also avoids extra logarithmic factors and holds both on average and with high probability.

arxiv:2611.26588.text: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards. From Ana E. Sanchez Villalobos and colleagues. Passing a regression can hide bugs when the scoreboard checks the reference model but misses a requirement in the specification. Verify the Verifier uses a large language model to check traces from passing tests directly against the specification. Across four OpenTitan blocks, it confirmed forty-one bugs as scoreboard escapes: each failed a new assertion on the buggy design, while the original design passed.

arxiv:2611.25640.text: Erasing the Wrong Thing: Conditional Attribute Leakage and Concept Erasure in Shared Foundation-Model Embeddings. From Haijun He and colleagues. Shared medical-image embeddings can leak sensitive traits, even after methods erase information across the whole dataset. The work proves that when a task and a sensitive trait are linked, global erasure cannot both remove trait information within each task group and preserve a nonzero linear task signal. It introduces Task-Conditional LEACE, which erases trait information separately within task groups. Across face attributes and chest radiographs, leakage remained after global erasure, while the new method recovered most of its lost task utility and kept within-group leakage close to the global method's level.

arxiv:2611.26092.text: Control of Complex Social Systems via Committed Minorities and Opinion Broadcast. From Roberta Raineri and colleagues. Social groups can be hard to steer because people's opinions and decisions shape each other. This chapter brings those changes together in a game-theoretic model, reviews when the model converges, and considers extensions for real-world features. It then examines two ways to guide the group: adding people who stick to a chosen view, or sending information to selected individuals. The approaches come with theoretical guarantees and are tested on examples and networks based on real-world data.

arxiv:2611.25124.text: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation. From Elijah Pelofske and colleagues. Quantum phase estimation can lose accuracy when it turns a continuous phase into a finite set of digital outcomes. This work learns an evolution time that makes the measured phase outcomes have low Shannon entropy. In numerical tests on quantum magnet models, minimizing that entropy greatly improves the accuracy of finding the minimum eigenvalue. The approach also enables shorter phase estimation circuits, which could make the method more practical for near-term scientific applications.

arxiv:2611.26136.text: Perturbation Algorithm and Iterative Realization of a Four-Layer Semi-Discrete Scheme for an Evolutionary Problem with a Variable Operator. From David Gulua and colleagues. Solving time-dependent evolution equations can be difficult when the operator changes over time. This work turns a third-order, four-step time scheme into three simpler two-step schemes, then solves each with iteration, requiring inversion only of a time-independent operator. The iterations converge at a geometric rate, with a ratio of order tau, and the method's error is shown to be of order tau cubed under a stated assumption. Numerical experiments illustrate the results.

arxiv:2611.26289.text: Causal Effect Estimation Under Uncertain Statistical Surrogacy. From Yi Liu and colleagues. Surrogate measures can make estimates of treatment effects more precise, but only when they reliably capture information about the main outcome. This work studies several possible surrogates, including cases where outcomes are missing, and examines how violations of that assumption affect bias and precision. The proposed method adaptively chooses among surrogate-based estimates while staying anchored to a robust benchmark. Simulations show a favorable balance between bias and variability across different degrees of assumption violation, and a clinical trial illustrates the approach.

arxiv:2611.25163.text: The low-degree sample complexity of clustering Gaussian mixtures with more groups than dimensions. From Alexandra Carpentier and colleagues. Clustering many Gaussian groups becomes difficult when there are more groups than dimensions: common distance-based and spectral methods need large separation, while tensor methods require many samples. For normally distributed group centers, this work matches a low-degree lower bound with an upper bound, up to subpolynomial factors. When the number of groups scales as the dimension raised to half of a real number greater than two, it identifies the sample size needed for clustering with very small separation. The bound is also sufficient when that real number is not an integer.

arxiv:2611.24979.text: Trace2ST: Recovering PLC Structured Text from I slash O Traces with LLM Generation and Verification. From Hsi Chang and colleagues. Industrial controllers often keep detailed input and output logs even when their original programs are lost, but rebuilding and checking the code is difficult. Trace2ST uses a large language model to write a candidate program, runs it cycle by cycle against the logs, and feeds mismatches back for up to three revisions. It exactly reproduces the recorded traces in forty-three of forty-seven cases and matches the original on ninety-four percent of scans for unseen inputs. Adding traces that exercise missed branches improves agreement on adversarial inputs, and tests on water-treatment data reveal the dataset's only actuator attack.

arxiv:2611.25252.text: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark. From Zhenling Chen and colleagues. Predictive maintenance models must generalize to equipment they have never seen, but published methods can depend heavily on how results are measured. In a benchmark spanning twenty-four datasets and fifty-eight held-out tests, leading coding agents beat automated machine learning and usually outperformed faithful versions of published methods. Their edge came from adapting a design to each machine's data, not from following a particular plan or using domain toolkits. Yet open-weight models often could not carry out those designs, suggesting generality is shifting from the model to the agent that builds it.

arxiv:2611.26239.text: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely. From Zheyuan Liu and colleagues. Robots can learn to refuse a prohibited task at the start, yet still carry it out if the task is already underway. Simply failing to finish is not enough: a robot may drop what it is holding. State-Aware Fallback Imitation teaches the robot to hold safely instead, using stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets at intermediate points in a task. In tests on LIBERO tasks, prohibited-task success after takeover fell to one point three percent, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while other task performance stayed high.

arxiv:2611.26073.text: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators. From Nagham Omar and colleagues. Deciding whether a language model can replace human annotators is difficult when different items are labeled by different people. AltRA-Test compares agreement in paired panels of human labels and mixed human and model labels, using resampling to account for the varying annotators. The test is statistically consistent, and in simulations it makes more correct replacement decisions than existing alternatives. Across real-world tasks, models pass in about half of the setups, showing that replacement depends on the task.

arxiv:2611.26601.text: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research. From Amine Lbath and colleagues. Claims about large language models finding and fixing software vulnerabilities are hard to compare, because evidence is scattered across research and industry reports. This study creates a framework to rate how independently agents work, and how reliable and well-supported each claim is. It finds that agents handled real vulnerabilities without human help before restricted frontier models appeared in twenty twenty-six, and that open models later matched them in discovery and validation. That year, disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, but the timing of fixes and attacks showed no noticeable change.

arxiv:2611.25654.text: DARSY: A Tool for Data-Driven Abstraction and Policy Synthesis for Stochastic Systems with Unknown Dynamics. From Thom Badings and colleagues. Verifying a stochastic system is difficult when its dynamics and noise distributions are unknown. DARSY builds a finite abstraction using simulated transitions and a bound on how quickly the dynamics can change, then uses robust dynamic programming to find a policy. It provides a lower bound on the chance that the system meets a specification, with a user-chosen confidence level. Its two-layer abstraction can reduce errors and give tighter guarantees than a standard abstraction.

arxiv:2611.25019.text: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities. From Masoud Gharahi. Many entanglement inequalities relate the entropies of groups of parties, but it has been unclear how the best coefficients depend on the pattern of cuts being compared. This work treats cuts as edges or hyperedges and derives sharp bounds from strong subadditivity and the properties of pure states, including conditions for equality. It finds the optimal coefficient for a broad family of weighted cuts and proves new sharp bounds for groups of different sizes. The results also connect equality and near-equality to multipartite entanglement, matrix product states, and estimates of recovery error.
